### 2026-10-04

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 58).** No variant is eligible, but this is the first lab or P7a trial to pass max DD ≤ 15%, PF ≥ 1.3 and ≥ 100 trades together. Every variant failed the same remaining condition: it did not beat total-return SPY (+351.4%, CAGR ≈ +7.9%).

| Variant | Return | CAGR | Max DD | PF | Trades | DSR | Failed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| TV10 (monthly) | +224.9% | +6.1% | 11.0% | 2.31 | 1,109 | 0.903 | beats SPY, DSR |
| TV12 (monthly) | +327.6% | +7.6% | 12.9% | 2.27 | 1,130 | 0.899 | beats SPY, DSR |
| TV10-W (weekly) | +129.7% | +4.3% | 10.6% | 1.49 | 2,602 | 0.703 | beats SPY, DSR |
| TV10-NOTREND | +198.4% | +5.7% | 18.0% | 1.77 | 1,411 | 0.758 | beats SPY, max DD, DSR |

**Hypothesis: half right.** Own-volatility scaling did fix the drawdown. F4-MOM12-N20-TREND's 22.2% fell to 11–13%, and 2008 is no longer the worst year for the trend-filtered variants (their worst year is 2015, at −2.3%). The return was cut too, from CAGR +16.2% to +6.1–7.6%. The second half of the expected failure ("the 10% target cuts CAGR below SPY TR") is what happened. The first half (a monthly scale too slow for a fast crash) did not: max DD stayed under 13%.

**Why.** A top-20 momentum book runs at roughly 20–25% annualized volatility, so a 10–12% target holds it at about half exposure most of the time, not only in crash spells. Combined with the SPY 200-day filter (cash in bear markets), the book is de-risked twice. The scale is capped at 1 (no leverage), so calm spells never make up the lost exposure. The return/drawdown trade is close to linear: TV10 → TV12 added +1.5 pts CAGR for +1.9 pts DD. Extrapolating, a target around 14% should land near SPY's CAGR with DD around 15%, which is right on the edge of the gate.

**Weekly re-ranking hurt.** TV10-W more than doubled trades (2,602), cut PF to 1.49 and CAGR to +4.3%. Faster re-scaling buys no drawdown (10.6% vs 11.0%) and pays for it in turnover and whipsaw. **The trend filter matters:** without it (TV10-NOTREND), own-vol scaling alone lets 2008 through (−13.8%, DD 18.0%). In this setup Barroso's scaling is not a substitute for the regime filter.

**DSR.** 0.90 for the monthly variants at N = 58, under 0.95 even before the SPY condition. The Sharpe (0.81) is good but not exceptional after deflation.

**What it teaches.** The frontier is now known to pass through DD ≈ 13% at CAGR ≈ SPY. Beating SPY at DD ≤ 15% needs either more return per unit of risk (a better signal), or a scale that de-risks only in crash regimes instead of all the time.

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-06

### 2026-10-06

## What this tried

The parent method (M0001) took the lab's best stock picker — buy the twenty strongest
twelve-month performers in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, and sit in cash whenever the market is
below its 200-day average — and shrank the whole book whenever it was risky, aiming to hold its
swings to a fixed 10–12% a year. That worked on the risk side and failed on the return side: the
worst fall dropped from 22.2% to 11–13%, but the growth rate dropped from 16.2% a year to
6.1–7.6%, under the 7.9% you would have got by just holding SPY.

The reason was blunt: a twenty-stock momentum book naturally swings about 20–25% a year, so a
10–12% ceiling holds it at roughly half invested **all the time**, not only in the dangerous
spells. This method keeps the ceiling but only switches it on when the book is unusually jumpy
**for itself**. It measures the book's swings over the last three months and compares them with
the middle value of that same measure over the last eighteen months. Below that normal level, the
book stays fully invested. Above it, the brake comes on.

Six versions were pre-registered: three that brake to a fixed ceiling once the trigger trips
(12%, 14%, and one that waits until swings are 1.25x normal), two that simply aim at the book's
own normal level instead of a fixed number, and one without the market filter to see what the
brake does on its own.

## The result

**Every version beat the market, by a lot.** Holding SPY with dividends over 1996–2015 turned
$1 into $4.51. The best version here turned it into $12.48.

| Version | Growth a year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Invested | Trades | Return per unit of fall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Brake to 12% above normal | +10.6% | 17.5% | 2.27 | 50% | 1,154 | 0.61 |
| Brake to 14% above normal | +11.6% | 17.7% | 2.29 | 53% | 1,157 | 0.66 |
| Brake to 12% above 1.25x normal | +13.5% | 21.8% | 2.25 | 59% | 1,160 | 0.62 |
| Aim at its own normal level | +13.6% | 21.2% | 2.25 | 59% | 1,150 | 0.64 |
| Aim at 85% of normal | **+12.6%** | **18.4%** | **2.33** | 53% | 1,148 | **0.68** |
| Brake to 12%, no market filter | +10.0% | 30.5% | 1.84 | 64% | 1,463 | 0.33 |
| *(SPY with dividends)* | *+7.9%* | *—* | *—* | *100%* | *—* | *—* |
| *(the unbraked picker, M0001's parent)* | *+16.2%* | *22.2%* | *2.27* | *67%* | *1,154* | *0.73* |

"Gains vs losses" is the profit factor: 2.33 means every dollar lost on bad trades was matched by
$2.33 made on good ones. "Invested" is the average share of the account actually in stocks; the
rest sat in cash. "Return per unit of fall" (MAR) is the growth rate divided by the worst fall —
one number for how much return each unit of pain bought.

**All six failed, on the same two conditions.** The worst fall is 17.5–21.8%, over the 15% limit.
And the deflated Sharpe — the measure of how likely a result is real rather than a lucky draw
after many tries — came in at 0.79–0.85 against the 0.95 the lab requires. Nothing here is
eligible to go live.

That said, this is the best the lab has produced. Five of the six now pass three of the five
conditions (beat the market, gains clearly outweigh losses, well over 100 trades), and miss only
the drawdown limit. The parent beat the market on none of its versions.

## Did the idea work?

**Half of it.** The return half worked exactly as hoped. Staying fully invested in calm spells
put the average money-at-work back up from M0001's 30–37% to 50–59%, and the growth rate came
back with it, from 6–7.6% to 10.6–13.6%. All of that gap to the market closed.

**The drawdown half did not.** The target was a worst fall under 15%; the answer was 17.5% at
best. I wrote down before the run that this was the likely failure, and that the fall would land
"at 18–22%". It landed at 17.5–21.8%.

## Why the falls survived

Look at *when* the money was lost. These strategies have almost no bad years at all: the worst
calendar year in twenty is −3.3%, and 2001, 2002 and 2008 come out flat, because the market filter
has them sitting in cash. The falls that matter happen inside good years. Measured month by month,
the four worst spells for the version that aims at 85% of normal are March–August 2006 (−11.7%),
June–August 1998 (−11.1%), April–June 2010 (−10.0%) and April–September 2011 (−8.5%); the version
that brakes to 12% has the same four in a different order, led by April–June 2010. (Those are
month-end numbers, so they are shallower than the 17.5–21.8% figures above, which are measured day
by day. The months are what identify the episodes.)

Those are not market crashes. In spring 2006 the market was comfortably above its 200-day
average, so the filter stayed switched on and invested, while the particular stocks momentum had
piled into — commodity and emerging-market names — reversed hard. And here is the problem: the
book's own three-month swing measure was still sitting near its normal level when that reversal
began, so the brake was off. It came on afterwards, once the damage was in the price.

**Measured volatility is a rear-view mirror.** The jump in volatility and the loss are the same
event. A three-month window needs weeks to register the jump, and by then the fall has happened.
That is why a brake tuned to volatility protects against *long* bad spells, which it did — nothing
here lost money in 2008 — and not against *sharp* ones, which is where the remaining 17–22% lives.

The version without the market filter settles the other half of the question. On its own the
brake is weak: the worst fall goes to 30.5% and 2008 costs 24.1%. The market filter, not the
volatility brake, is what keeps the strategy out of real crashes. The parent found the same thing.

## The uncomfortable comparison

Set the versions side by side with how much money each one actually kept in stocks:

| | Invested | Growth per unit invested | Worst fall per unit invested |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| The unbraked picker | 67% | 24.2 | 33.2 |
| M0001, braked all the time (12%) | 37% | 20.6 | 34.9 |
| This method, aim at 85% of normal | 53% | 23.7 | 34.7 |
| This method, brake to 12% above normal | 50% | 21.3 | 35.1 |

The right-hand column barely moves. Every version, braked or not, gives up about the same amount
of drawdown for each unit of money it puts at work. In other words the brake is not removing
risk so much as **turning the whole position down** — less money in, proportionally less return
and proportionally less pain. There is no free lunch in it.

The middle column is where this method earns its keep. At 53% invested it produced 23.7 units of
growth per unit invested, against M0001's 20.6 — and nearly the 24.2 of the unbraked original.
So braking *only when the book is jumpy for itself* is a genuinely better-targeted brake than
braking all the time. It is just a second-order improvement on top of a first-order dial.

Because the trade is so nearly proportional, the line can be read off. The versions run from
(11.0% fall, +6.1% growth) at the cautious end to (22.2% fall, +16.2%) at the bold end, and it
crosses a 15% fall at about +9 to +10% growth a year. That is still above the market's 7.9%. So a
setting between this method's mildest version and M0001's should land inside the drawdown limit
*and* beat the market — the first time anything in this lab has.

## The ceiling nobody can dial past

That would still not be eligible, because of the deflated Sharpe. The lab has now run 85 trials,
and the more things you try, the better a result has to be before it counts as more than the best
of 85 coin flips. Holding everything else at this method's shape, the Sharpe ratio needed to clear
0.95 works out at about **1.0 a year**. The best this lab has ever recorded is 0.89, from the
unbraked picker. This method's best is 0.87.

And the brake does not help there. Across the whole family — unbraked 0.89, braked all the time
0.81, braked only when jumpy 0.87 — the Sharpe hardly moves, and when it moves it moves down.
That is the same proportionality as above, seen from another angle: turning the position up and
down changes return and risk together, and leaves the ratio between them alone.

So the drawdown limit can be reached by dialing. The deflated Sharpe cannot. It needs a better
*signal* — stocks picked in a way that earns more per unit of risk — not a better brake on this
one. Roughly 70 more trials costs another 0.06 of deflated Sharpe at a fixed quality, so the bar
rises as the lab keeps searching.

(Those Sharpe figures use a representative shape for the distribution of daily returns rather than
each trial's own; treat 1.0 as "about one", not a precise threshold.)

## Compared with the parent and the near misses

Against M0001: much better on return (+10.6 to +13.6% a year against +6.1 to +7.6%), worse on
drawdown (17.5–21.8% against 11.0–12.9%), the same gains-to-losses ratio (2.3), and a better
return per unit of fall (0.61–0.68 against 0.56–0.59). The hypothesis that the parent's problem
was constant de-risking rather than de-risking as such is confirmed.

Against the best near miss, the unbraked picker at 0.73 return per unit of fall: still behind.
Nothing in the lab has yet beaten simply running that picker as it is and accepting a 22% fall.

## My opinion

This direction is worth two more trials, and then it should be retired.

The first is cheap and I think it will land: take the mildest setting here and tighten it one
notch — aim at about 70% of the book's own normal level of swings, or brake to a 10% ceiling with
a trigger that trips a little earlier. The line says that lands near a 15% worst fall with growth
around +9 to +10% a year, which would be the lab's first result to clear the drawdown limit while
beating the market. It is interpolation along a line I have already measured, not a new idea, so
it should be run once, recorded, and not tuned further; and it will still fail the deflated
Sharpe.

The second is the one I actually care about. The falls here happen in calm markets, and a
volatility brake arrives late by construction. The obvious replacement is a brake that watches the
book's *own price path* rather than its volatility: cut exposure when the basket of stocks
currently held is some distance below its own recent high, and restore it when the basket recovers.
That reacts on the first day of a reversal rather than six weeks in, and it would attack the
spring-2006 and spring-2010 episodes directly, which volatility cannot. I have queued it.

What I would not do is keep adjusting the volatility brake. The evidence in this run is that the
whole family — braked, unbraked, braked cleverly — lies on one straight line, and every trial
spent on it moves along the line rather than off it, while raising the bar for everything that
comes after. The remaining problem in this lab is not risk management. It is that the best signal
it has earns a Sharpe of 0.89 and needs about 1.0. That is a stock-picking problem, and the
queued work on residual momentum and on covariance-aware weighting is where I would spend the
next runs.
methods.verdict: Braking only when the book is jumpy for itself beat the market on all six versions (+10.6 to +13.6% a year vs +7.9%, gains 2.3x losses) — but the worst fall stayed at 17.5-21.8%, because the falls happen in calm markets before volatility rises.

methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-06

## What this tried

M0001 asked whether scaling a momentum book by its own recent volatility could tame momentum's
crashes. Its monthly version was the best thing the lab had found: gains outweighed losses 2.31
to 1, and it never lost more than 11.0% from a peak. Its weekly version, which re-did everything
once a week, collapsed to 1.49 and more than doubled its trading.

The weekly version changed two things at once — **which** stocks it held, and **how much** of
them it held. So nobody could say which change did the damage. This method separated them. The
engine gained a new control that lets a rule set pick its stocks on one clock and set its
exposure on another, and the five variants here walk that grid.

## The result

Nothing here beat the market. Buying and holding SPY over the same 1996–2015 stretch returned
+351%, and the best variant here returned +159%. All five failed on that alone.

The comparison that matters is against M0001's own two versions:

| How it picks stocks | How it sets exposure | Gains vs losses | Trading | Worst fall | Growth rate | Return per unit of fall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| monthly | monthly (M0001-TV10) | 2.31 | 2.74 | 11.0% | 6.14% | 0.56 |
| monthly | weekly (M0004-TV10-MW) | 1.81 | 3.17 | 10.3% | 4.80% | 0.47 |
| monthly | daily (M0004-TV10-MD) | 1.90 | 3.67 | 10.1% | 4.92% | 0.49 |
| weekly | weekly (M0001-TV10-W) | 1.49 | 5.93 | 10.6% | 4.29% | 0.40 |
| weekly | daily (M0004-TV10-WD) | 1.53 | 6.62 | 11.5% | 4.42% | 0.38 |

("Gains vs losses" is profit factor: 2.31 means winners brought in 2.31 dollars for every dollar
the losers gave back. "Trading" is turnover: how many times over the book was replaced per year.
"Return per unit of fall" is MAR, growth rate divided by worst fall — higher is better.)

## The hypothesis half held

I predicted that re-picking stocks weekly, not re-sizing weekly, was what doubled the trading.
**That part is right, and clearly so.** Holding the stock-picking clock at monthly and speeding
the exposure clock up from monthly to weekly to daily moved trading only 2.74 → 3.17 → 3.67.
Moving the stock-picking clock from monthly to weekly moved it 2.74 → 5.93. Re-picking stocks
costs about eight times as much trading as re-sizing does. The feature does exactly what it was
built to do, and it isolates the cost cleanly.

**The rest of the prediction was wrong.** I expected that removing the churn would bring the
result back near the monthly version's 2.31. It did not: it landed at 1.81. Faster risk checks
cost half a point of profit factor while adding only 0.43 of turnover, so the loss is not a
trading-cost story.

My written expected failure — "turnover lands near 5 and the profit factor near 1.49" — did not
happen either. Turnover stayed low. The result still got worse.

## Why

The thing being measured moves too slowly for the question to matter. The exposure comes from
three months of realised volatility. A three-month average barely changes in a week, so
re-reading it every Monday returns almost the same number it returned a month ago. The faster
clock buys essentially no new information.

What it does buy is more occasions to act on noise. Each re-check compares the book to a new
target and trades the difference whenever it exceeds 1% of equity. A slightly different number,
checked four times as often, nudges the book back and forth around the same level. Average
exposure drifted down from 29.9% to 27.2%, growth fell from 6.1% to 4.8%, and the worst fall
improved by only 0.7 of a point — from 11.0% to 10.3%. Return per unit of fall got *worse*, 0.56
to 0.47. Faster risk control cut the returns more than it cut the risk.

The sharpest evidence is the variant with no trend filter. Measured monthly it scored 1.77 with
a worst fall of 18.0%; measured weekly it scored 1.77 with a worst fall of 17.2%. Identical.
Without the market-trend filter in front of it, re-checking volatility weekly does nothing at
all. So the small effect the other variants show is not the volatility signal reacting faster —
it is an interaction with the trend filter, and it runs the wrong way.

## How likely is this real

Not likely, and it does not need to be: nothing passed. After 69 recorded attempts, the lab's
luck-adjusted confidence for these five sits between 0.59 and 0.73, where 0.95 is the bar. Even
the headline comparison against M0001 should be read as one clean mechanical result — re-picking
drives turnover, re-sizing does not — rather than as five precise numbers.

The worst years were mild: 2015 at −5.1% for the headline variant, 2006 at −2.1% for the daily
one. The no-trend-filter variant lost 14.0% in 2008 and breached the 15% drawdown limit at
17.2%, the same way its monthly parent did.

## My opinion:

This direction is finished, and the feature that came out of it is worth more than the result
did. The cadence split works and it answered the question it was built for in one run: the
turnover penalty belongs to re-ranking, not to re-sizing. That is a reusable fact and the
control now exists for any future method that wants it.

But re-checking a three-month volatility estimate more often was never going to help, and I
should have seen that before spending a method id on it. The lesson generalises: the useful
re-check rate is set by the signal's own timescale, not by how often we are willing to trade. A
three-month average wants a monthly clock. Pairing a slow signal with a fast clock adds cost and
no information.

What I would try next is the opposite pairing: keep the monthly stock picking, but drive the
exposure from something that genuinely moves week to week, so the fast clock has something to
react to. Short-window realised volatility (around 20 days) or a drawdown-triggered cut would
both qualify. That is a real test of "faster risk control helps", which this run did not
actually perform — it tested "re-reading a slow number faster helps", and the answer is no.

I would not spend another id on splitting cadences with a slow signal.
methods.verdict: The split works and proves re-ranking drives the turnover, not re-sizing — but re-reading a three-month volatility weekly adds cost and no information, and nothing beat SPY.

methods.hypothesis: Every lab method so far ranks on price alone. The four fundamental factor families with the longest out-of-sample record - book-to-price, return on equity, gross profitability and standardized unexpected earnings - are now available point in time from EDGAR, with each fact gated on its filed date. ### 2026-10-05

# M0005: the six trials measure data coverage, not the factor premia

MEASURED after the run. The dev window is 1996-01-03..2015-10-16 (19.8 years). The fundamental
panel this run loaded covers **2015-01-06..2015-10-16 -- about 9 months, 4% of the window**.
For the other 19 years `as_of` returned nothing, the eligibility gate found fewer than 20 names,
and the book held cash. Every "failed: beats SPY TR; >= 100 trades" line is that, not a verdict
on book-to-price, ROE, gross profitability or SUE.

The tell is in the numbers: 15-32 trades over 19.8 years (the gate wants >= 100), CAGR +0.2% at
maxDD 8-13%, and "worst year 1996 +0.0%" -- a year in which the strategy could not have held
anything.

## Why the panel is 9 months and not 13 years

Two cuts compose, and neither is visible from the store manifest:

1. The ingest kept facts filed on or after 2013-01-01. Raw `fundamental_facts` holds
   1,228,822 rows filed 2013-01-02..2026-10-02.
2. The panel is `fundamental_facts` JOINED to `ticker_cik` **by date**, and every `ticker_cik`
   interval starts on or after 2015-01-02, because the set's scope predicate is "ever-members
   since 2015-01-02". So the join drops the **181,491 facts filed before 2015-01-02** outright,
   and nothing before 2015 has a map row to join to at all.

So the panel could not have reached further back than 2015-01-02 however the ingest was run.

## The structural finding, which outlives this method

**This lab's dev window and XBRL's availability barely overlap.** The window opens in 1996;
XBRL starts ~2009 and, after the CIK map's 2015-01-02 scope, the usable panel starts 2015.
A fundamental-factor method cannot be evaluated on the dev window as it stands. That is not a
property of M0005 -- it is a property of the lab, and any future fundamentals method hits it.

Three ways out, none of them free:
- Re-vendor `ticker_cik.csv` with intervals extended back to each symbol's actual first
  membership (not 2015-01-02), which buys 2013-2014 -- still 2.8 of 19.8 years.
- Give fundamentals methods their own shorter dev window, which breaks comparability with the
  64 trials recorded against 1996-2015 and the DSR's N.
- Accept that these premia are testable only on the post-2015 window, which is the held-out
  test window this lab has deliberately never used.

## What the gate should have been

The runbook's gate -- "does the store manifest list fundamentals.csv" -- is necessary and not
sufficient. It is binary where the risk is continuous: a store can carry a panel that covers
4% of the window and pass. The gate a future method needs is **coverage**: the fraction of
rebalance dates in the dev window for which `as_of` returns a snapshot for at least the
eligibility minimum. Had that been checked here it would have read ~4% and the run should
not have happened.

The run was pre-flighted by sampling `as_of(2015-06-30)`, which returned 400/400 snapshots --
a date inside the covered sliver. Sampling one date inside the data is not a coverage check.

## Status

`rejected` stands as the recorded outcome, and the six `config_digest`s are spent. The
hypothesis itself is **untested**, not refuted. Re-test as a variation (`source_kind='variation'`,
`parent_id='M0005'`) once one of the three ways out above is chosen -- `runner.preflight`
permits exactly that, and the digests will differ because the window or the map will.


### 2026-10-05

# Correction: the coverage measurement, done properly

My first note said the panel covered ~9 months of the dev window. Measured correctly it is
worse, and the first measurement's METHOD was wrong in a way worth recording.

`panel.as_of(symbol, t)` **always returns a Snapshot** -- an empty husk with
`observations == {}` when no fact is known yet. It never returns None. So
`sum(1 for s in syms if panel.as_of(s, t) is not None)` counts every symbol in every year and
measures nothing. That is exactly the check I pre-flighted this run with ("400/400 snapshots at
2015-06-30"), and it would have reported 780/780 for 1996 just as happily.

The correct test is whether the snapshot carries observations:

    n = sum(1 for sym in panel.symbols
            if (snap := panel.as_of(sym, t)) is not None and snap.observations)

## What that actually reports

    1996-06-30 ..  2014-06-30:    0 of 780 rankable   (sampled every 2 years -- all zero)
    2015-01-28 :   25 of 780
    2015-02-28 :  428 of 780
    2015-03-28 :  489 of 780
    2015-06-28 :  507 of 780
    2015-10-28 :  521 of 780

So the dev window is 1996-01-03..2015-10-16 and the panel can rank **nobody at all** until
2015-01, reaching ~507 of 780 by mid-2015. The book held cash for **19 of 19.8 years**, then
had roughly eight months of signal. The six trials measure that, and nothing about the premia.

This also sharpens the earlier claim: it is not that coverage was thin, it is that coverage was
**zero** for 96% of the window. A method ranking the top 20 of an empty eligible set targets
nothing, which is why 15-32 trades appeared where the gate wanted 100.

## The lesson that generalises

A "does the file exist" gate and a "does `as_of` return something" gate are both vacuous here,
for the same underlying reason: the fundamentals layer answers every query, and encodes "I know
nothing yet" as empty content rather than as an absent result. That is a defensible design --
it is what lets `Market` carry `EMPTY_PANEL` and every allocator keep working -- but it means
**presence is never evidence of coverage** anywhere in this subsystem. Check content.

`docs/runbooks/data-pipeline.md` now carries the corrected snippet under "The lab and
fundamentals", with this failure written next to it.

### 2026-10-06

### 2026-10-06

**The idea in one line.** Instead of ranking stocks on how much they went up over the last year,
rank them on how much they went up *after taking out the part the whole market explains*. The
market's own move is stripped from every stock's return first; what is left is the stock's own
story, and that is what gets ranked.

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 85 trials at run time).** Nothing is eligible:
every variant failed the 15% drawdown limit. But one of them, the unscaled version, is now the
best risk-adjusted result the lab has ever produced.

| Variant | Total return | CAGR | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Top 20, scaled | +650% | +10.7% | 16.9% | 1.84 | 1,734 | 0.81 | 0.64 | 0.78 | worst fall |
| Top 10, scaled | +572% | +10.1% | 19.7% | 1.73 | 959 | 0.70 | 0.51 | 0.61 | worst fall |
| Top 30, scaled | +667% | +10.8% | 17.3% | 2.01 | 2,368 | 0.87 | 0.63 | 0.86 | worst fall |
| **Top 20, unscaled** | **+1,502%** | **+15.0%** | **19.6%** | **2.16** | **1,596** | **0.94** | **0.77** | **0.91** | worst fall |
| Top 20, no market-trend gate | +547% | +9.9% | 51.0% | 1.45 | 2,332 | 0.57 | 0.19 | 0.40 | worst fall |

Buying and holding SPY over the same window returned +351% (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the
deepest peak-to-bottom loss; the rule is that it must stay at or under 15%. "Gains vs losses"
(profit factor) is total winnings divided by total losses; it must be at least 1.3. "Return per
unit of fall" (MAR) is yearly return divided by worst fall — the lab's headline ranking number.
"Luck score" (DSR) is how likely the result is real rather than a fluke after this many tries;
it must reach 0.95.

The method this one was built to beat is the top-20 yearly-momentum book with the same market
trend gate: it made 16.2% a year with a 22.2% worst fall, 0.73 return per unit of fall.

**Did the hypothesis hold? Partly, and not the way I expected.**

Yes, stripping the market out of the signal lowered the worst fall without cutting how much money
is invested. The unscaled version holds just as much stock as the old one (67% of the time
invested, versus 67%) and still cut the worst fall from 22.2% to 19.6%, for only 1.2 points of
yearly return. That is the cheapest drawdown reduction this lab has found: 2.6 points of fall
removed for 1.2 points of return, a rate of 0.46. Every other way of cutting the fall has cost
more: shrinking the position size to hit a volatility target cost about 0.8 points of return per
point of fall, and the scaling inside this very method cost 1.6.

No, it did not get anywhere near the 15% limit. 19.6% is still 4.6 points over, and the gap is
not closeable by this lever alone.

**Did the expected failure happen? Yes, exactly, and it is the most useful thing here.** I wrote
in advance that dividing the residual by its own wobble would tilt the book toward quiet,
low-drift names and cost return. It did. The only difference between the top-20 scaled and the
top-20 unscaled version is that one division. It took yearly return from 15.0% down to 10.7% and
the worst fall from 19.6% down to 16.9%. So the famous "idiosyncratic momentum" scaling from the
papers is, in a long-only book, just another way of buying a smaller drawdown with return — and a
poor-value one at that. The raw residual is the part that works.

**The no-trend-gate run is a clean refutation, and it matters.** The papers say residual momentum
largely cures the momentum crash. Run without the market trend gate, this book fell 51% and lost
34% in 2008. The old total-return book, run the same way, is no better. The reason is that the
papers measure a long-and-short momentum portfolio, whose crash really is a momentum-specific
event. A book that only buys has a completely different problem: its drawdown is the *market's*
drawdown, and no amount of cleaning up the ranking signal removes that. Only being out of the
market removes it. So for us, residual momentum is a stock-picking improvement, not a crash cure.

**Worst year and when the fall happened.** For every trend-gated variant the worst year is 2015
(−2.9% for the unscaled version, −4.7% for the scaled one) — the window ends mid-October 2015,
in the middle of that year's correction. The deepest fall was not 2008 or 2000 at all: it was the
three months after June 1998, the Russia/LTCM squeeze, when the market dropped about 19% in six
weeks and the 200-day trend gate had not yet turned off. 2001, 2002 and 2008 are all flat (+0%)
because the gate kept the book in cash through them. That tells us where the remaining 4.6 points
of drawdown live: not in long bear markets, which the gate already handles, but in one fast shock
the gate reacts to too late.

**Why the return is lower than total momentum, and where it is not.** Splitting the window in
half is revealing:

| | 1996–2002 | 2003–2015 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Total-return momentum, top 20 | +22.6%/yr | +13.0%/yr |
| Residual momentum, top 20 unscaled | +15.0%/yr | +15.1%/yr |

Total momentum's whole advantage comes from 1999–2000, where it made +62% and +43% against the
residual book's +56% and +21%. That is precisely the beta being stripped out: in the dot-com run
the biggest winners were the highest-beta technology names, and total momentum rode them because
their market exposure was part of the signal. Residual momentum deliberately refuses to. In the
thirteen years since 2002 the residual book is the better one, +15.1% a year against +13.0%, and
it is far steadier — the same 15% in both halves, against 22.6% then 13.0%. I would rather own
the steady one, but I am wary of leaning on a two-way split of one window, so I am recording this
as an observation and not as a reason to prefer it.

**Luck score.** The unscaled top-20 scores 0.91 after 85 trials — the highest the lab has reached,
above the 0.90 of the volatility-scaled momentum book, and still short of the 0.95 bar. In plain
words: after 85 attempts, there is roughly a 9% chance a result this good is the best of 85 coin
flips rather than a real edge. The Sharpe ratio of 0.94 is the highest in the lab too. Note that
the scaled variants are *worse* on this measure (0.61–0.86), which is further evidence that the
scaling adds nothing.

**Book size barely matters.** Top 10, 20 and 30 of the scaled signal all land between 10.1% and
10.8% a year with falls between 16.9% and 19.7%. Thirty names is slightly the best of the three
on gains-versus-losses (2.01) and on luck score (0.86), which fits: more names, less single-name
noise. But the spread is small enough that book size is not the lever here.

**My opinion:** this direction is worth more trials, and it is the most promising thread in the
lab right now. The finding that matters is not that residual momentum passed — it did not — but
that it is the first lever found that cuts the worst fall at a *discount* rather than at full
price: 2.6 points of drawdown for 1.2 points of return, where everything else has charged one for
one or worse. That is a better starting book, not a finished method. What I would try next, and
what I have queued, is to take the unscaled top-20 residual book exactly as it stands and put the
volatility-target overlay on top of it — the same one that took the old momentum book from 22.2%
down to 12.9%. On that lever's historical exchange rate, pulling 19.6% down to about 14% should
cost roughly 4 points of yearly return, landing near 11% a year against SPY's 7.9%, with the fall
inside the limit. That would be eligible. It is the first combination in this lab where the
arithmetic actually closes, because residual momentum hands the overlay a book with 15% of return
to spend instead of 16.2% at a 22.2% fall. The second thing I would try, and have also queued, is
a faster exit for the one shock that actually caused the damage: the 200-day gate was too slow in August 1998, and a shorter or two-speed gate on the same book is the cheapest way to
attack the remaining 4.6 points. What I would *not* spend another trial on is the stdev scaling
from the papers, or the no-gate configuration; both are now settled, in opposite directions.
methods.verdict: Stripping the market's move out of the ranking is the lab's cheapest drawdown cut yet - 15.0% a year at a 19.6% worst fall, the best return-per-fall on record - but still 4.6 points over the limit, and the textbook scaling that was supposed to help only costs return.

methods.name: Minimum-variance weighting of the momentum book
methods.sourceRef: Clarke, de Silva & Thorley (2006), Minimum-variance portfolios in the U.S. equity market, JPM 33(1); Ledoit & Wolf (2004), A well-conditioned estimator for large-dimensional covariance matrices, J. Multivariate Analysis 88(2)
methods.hypothesis: F4-MOM12-N20-TREND beat SPY TR (CAGR +16.2% vs +7.9%, PF 2.27) and failed only on max DD (22.2%); M0001 cut that drawdown to 11-13% but only by holding cash, which cost so much return that CAGR fell to 6-7.6%, below SPY. Keeping the same names at full exposure and setting their relative weights to minimise portfolio variance under a Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrix (long only, per-name cap) should cut max DD below 15% through diversification rather than through cash, leaving CAGR above SPY TR.

Failing that, the covariance estimate is backward-looking and tilts the book toward names that were calm and are about to break, trading 2-4 pts of CAGR for only 2-3 pts of drawdown -- the same near-linear frontier M0001 found, reached a different way.

### 2026-10-06

### 2026-10-06

**What was tried.** Keep exactly the names the best momentum method already picks — the 20 stocks
with the strongest 12-month gains, held only while the market is above its 200-day average — but
stop splitting the money evenly between them. Instead, work out from the last year of daily prices
how the 20 move *together*, and pick the mix of them that wobbles least. The money stays fully
invested; only the split between the names changes. The idea was that M0001 had to hold half its
money in cash to calm the ride, and cash costs return. Spreading cleverly instead of holding cash
should calm the ride for free.

**Result (1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 74).** It beat the market by a wide margin and still failed,
on the same condition as everything before it: the worst fall was too deep.

| Variant | Total return | CAGR | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | DSR | Failed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| C10 (20 names, 10% cap) | +1,174% | +13.7% | 21.6% | 1.96 | 983 | 0.850 | worst fall, DSR |
| C15 (20 names, 15% cap) | +1,046% | +13.1% | 22.7% | 1.94 | 899 | 0.831 | worst fall, DSR |
| C10-H126 (6-month history) | +1,143% | +13.6% | 21.5% | 1.96 | 1,005 | 0.842 | worst fall, DSR |
| N30-C07 (30 names, 7% cap) | +727% | +11.3% | 20.0% | 2.14 | 1,223 | 0.817 | worst fall, DSR |
| C10-NOTREND (no market filter) | +1,000% | +12.9% | **54.0%** | 1.51 | 1,287 | 0.599 | worst fall, DSR |

Buying and holding SPY with its dividends made +351% over the same years, a CAGR of +7.9%. So the
best variant earned about 1.7 times SPY's yearly rate. The limit it breaks is the 15% worst-fall
rule: at its worst the book was 21.6% below its previous high, 6.6 points too deep. "CAGR" is the
steady yearly rate that would produce the same end result. "Gains vs losses" (profit factor) of 1.96
means every $1 lost on losing trades was matched by $1.96 made on winning ones.

**DSR 0.850 at N = 74.** The lab has now run 74 experiments. The deflated Sharpe ratio asks: given
that we have tried 74 things, how confident can we be that this one is genuinely good rather than
the luckiest of 74 coin-flips? It says about 85% confident. The bar is 95%. So even setting the
drawdown aside, this is not yet a result to stake money on. Note that it is the *highest* DSR any
market-beating book in this lab has reached; the ones that cleared 0.90 (M0001) did so by being
safe and slow, not by being good.

**The hypothesis was wrong, and in an interesting way.** The weighting did exactly what it was
designed to do: the book's year-to-year wobble (annualised volatility of monthly returns) fell from
16.2% to 13.3% — an 18% reduction — while the money invested stayed the same (68% of the account on
average, identical to the equal-weight book). The mathematics worked. The problem is that the
wobble is not what the 15% rule measures. **The worst fall barely moved at all: 22.2% to 21.6%.**
Volatility and drawdown turned out to be two different risks, and this method only touches one of
them.

**Why.** The worst fall is not a stormy stretch of ordinary wobble. It is one specific event, and it
is the same event for every trend-filtered variant: March to August 2006. In those months SPY fell
at worst 7.6% and never once dropped below its 200-day average, so the market filter kept the book
fully invested throughout. What crashed was not the market — it was momentum itself. The commodity
and emerging-market names that had climbed smoothly for a year all unwound together. The
equal-weight book went from +8.4% to −10.9% over those five months. No way of re-splitting money
*between* those 20 names can help, because all 20 were the same bet.

Worse, the clever weighting made 2006 *worse*, not better. By May the min-variance book was already
down 3.5% while the equal-weight book was still up 0.6%. The reason is the heart of the matter: the
optimiser leans toward the names that have been calm over the past year, and in 2006 the calmest
momentum names were exactly the smooth one-way climbers that broke hardest. A year of calm upward
drift looks like safety to a covariance matrix and is in fact a crowded trade. **Past calm is not
future safety when the calm came from a trend.**

**The no-filter variant settles the argument.** Strip out the market filter and leave only the
min-variance weighting as the safety net, and the book falls 54.0% at its worst and loses 40.9% in
2008 — a hair worse than simply holding SPY through the crash. The same test on M0001 (own-volatility
scaling, no filter) lost 18.0% at its worst and 13.8% in 2008. Holding *less* protects you in a
crash. Holding the *same amount more cleverly spread* protects you not at all.

**Was it concentration?** No — checked directly. The 10% cap held: on sample dates the book's
effective breadth was 12 to 13 names out of 16 actually held (equal weight would be 16), with the
cap binding on 4 to 8 of them. It never collapsed into a handful of stocks. The 15% cap let it
concentrate more (effective breadth 10 to 11) and did measurably worse on every count, which is
consistent: the optimiser's conviction is not worth following.

**What breadth did do.** Across the whole family, the worst fall falls steadily as the book holds
more names — 5 names: 33.0%, 10 names: 28.2%, 20 names: 22.2%, 30 names: 20.0% — and the yearly
rate falls with it. The 30-name variant was the only one whose worst moment moved away from 2006
(to the 1998 Russia/LTCM selloff), lost the least in 2006 of any variant, and had the best
gains-vs-losses ratio of the five at 2.14. Plain breadth bought more drawdown relief than the
covariance mathematics did. But the curve is flattening: going from 20 to 30 names bought 2.2 points
of drawdown and cost 2.4 points of yearly return, and extending it to 15% would cost more return
than there is to give.

**Expected failure: the first half happened exactly.** It was written in advance that "momentum's
top 20 are a single crowded bet… there is no low-correlation corner for the optimiser to hide in
and the worst fall stays near 20%." That is precisely the result, 21.6%. The second half (a
backward-looking covariance tilting toward names about to break) also happened, in 2006, and cost
2.5 points of yearly return for 0.6 points of drawdown — a far worse trade than M0001's, which gave
up 1.5 points of return per 1.9 points of drawdown. Scaling exposure down is roughly four times
more efficient at buying drawdown than re-weighting is.

**Against the parent and the near misses.** The parent, equal-weight top-20 momentum, earned +16.2%
a year with a 22.2% worst fall (MAR 0.73). This method earned +13.7% with a 21.6% worst fall (MAR
0.64). It is strictly worse: it paid 2.5 points of yearly return for 0.6 points of safety and 34%
more trading (turnover 8.06 against 6.01, because the weights move every month even when the names
do not). M0001, the other child of the same parent, reached an 12.9% worst fall but only +7.6% a
year, just under SPY. Between them the two children now bracket the problem: one bought safety too
expensively, the other bought almost none at all.

**My opinion:** this direction is finished, and I would not spend another trial on weighting schemes
inside the momentum book. The evidence is unusually clean — the weighting worked as mathematics
(volatility down 18%) and failed as risk control (drawdown down 3%), because the drawdown that binds
is a single factor unwind in which every holding is the same bet. Risk-parity, equal-risk-contribution
and hierarchical-risk-parity weighting would all hit the same wall for the same reason, so I would
skip them too. What this run genuinely established is where the real problem lives, and it is not
where anyone was looking: the 200-day market filter is blind to a momentum crash. In 2006 it held the
book fully invested while the book fell 18%, and 2006 — not 2008, not 2000 — is the event that has
blocked every momentum method in this lab. So the next trial should gate the book on its *own*
drawdown rather than on the market's trend: when the momentum book is more than some threshold below
its own high-water mark, cut exposure until it recovers. That attacks the exact failure, costs nothing
in the calm years where M0001's permanent half-exposure bled return, and is the one lever nothing in
the lab has pulled yet. I have queued it. As a cheap second, a plain equal-weight breadth sweep
(30, 40, 50 names) is worth one run to see where the breadth-versus-return curve actually bends,
since breadth outperformed the optimiser at the one job the optimiser was hired for.
methods.verdict: Clever weighting cut the wobble 18% but the worst fall only 3% (21.6%), and cost 2.5 pts of yearly return: the drawdown that binds is a 2006 momentum crash the market filter never saw

methods.name: De-risk on the book's own drawdown, not the market's trend
methods.hypothesis: Every trend-filtered momentum book in the lab has its max DD in the SAME five months, 2006-03 to 2006-08, and the SPY 200-day gate was INVESTED throughout (SPY fell at most 7.6% and never broke its SMA): the binding event is a momentum-factor unwind the market filter cannot see. M0001 fixed it by holding ~50% cash all the time, which cost 8.6 pts of CAGR; M0008 tried to fix it by reweighting inside the book and bought 0.6 pts of DD for 2.5 pts of CAGR. Neither is targeted. Instead keep F4-MOM12-N20-TREND at full exposure and add a SECOND gate on the book's OWN equity curve: when the strategy's own high-water mark is more than d% above its current equity, scale exposure to k (or zero) until a new high is made. This is state the allocator can compute from its own targets' trailing returns (a synthetic equal-weight basket curve of the held names), so it needs no new data. It costs nothing in the calm years where M0001 bled return, and it fires in exactly the 2006-style factor unwind that the SPY gate misses. Variants: trigger 8/12/15%, re-entry on a new high vs a fixed recovery fraction, and partial (50%) vs full de-risking.

methods.name: Breadth as the drawdown control: equal-weight momentum at 30, 40 and 50 names
methods.hypothesis: Across the F4 and M0008 families max DD falls monotonically with the number of names held - 5: 33.0%, 10: 28.2%, 20: 22.2%, ~30 (M0008-N30-C07): 20.0% - while CAGR falls with it (17.5%, 18.0%, 16.2%, 11.3%). methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-06

**The idea in one line.** Take the lab's best stock-picking book so far (the "residual momentum"
book: buy the 20 stocks whose own rise, after removing the market's move, was strongest over the
past year) and put a volatility brake on it: when the 20 stocks together have been swinging hard,
hold less of them and keep the rest in cash.

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 90 trials at run time).** Nothing is formally
eligible, but this is a first for the lab: **two versions pass every one of the owner's go-live
rules on the test bench** — beat SPY, worst fall at or under 15%, gains at least 1.3x losses,
at least 100 trades. The only thing they miss is the luck score (DSR), the lab's own extra bar.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Top 20, brake at 12% swing | +359% | +8.0% | 13.3% | 1.96 | 1,575 | 0.84 | 0.60 | 0.81 | luck score |
| Top 20, brake at 14% swing | +478% | +9.3% | 15.4% | 1.97 | 1,583 | 0.84 | 0.60 | 0.82 | worst fall (by 0.4), luck score |
| Top 20, brake at 16% swing | +652% | +10.7% | 16.3% | 2.03 | 1,587 | 0.88 | 0.66 | 0.86 | worst fall, luck score |
| Top 30, brake at 14% swing | +433% | +8.8% | 16.2% | 2.01 | 2,184 | 0.84 | 0.54 | 0.82 | worst fall, luck score |
| **Top 20, brake at 14%, one-month swing reading** | **+660%** | **+10.8%** | **14.1%** | **2.03** | **1,588** | **0.93** | **0.76** | **0.90** | luck score |
| *Parent: top 20, no brake* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.94* | *0.77* | *0.91* | *worst fall* |

Buying and holding SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year).
"Worst fall" is the deepest drop from a peak; it must stay at or under 15%. "Gains vs losses"
(profit factor) is total winnings over total losses. "Return per unit of fall" (MAR) is yearly
return divided by worst fall. "Luck score" (DSR) is how likely the result is real rather than the
best of 90 lucky tries; it must reach 0.95.

**The standout: the one-month version.** It made 10.8% a year against SPY's 7.9%, lost at most
14.1% from a peak (inside the 15% limit by 0.9 points), won 2.03 dollars for every dollar lost,
and traded 1,588 times. Its return per unit of fall, 0.76, is essentially the parent's 0.77, which
means the brake cost almost nothing in efficiency: it just ran the same book smaller, and smaller
*at the right times*. Its luck score is 0.90: after 90 attempts there is roughly a one-in-ten
chance that a result this good is luck. Not good enough for the bar, but the second-highest the
lab has seen, behind only its own parent.

**Did the hypothesis hold? Mostly, but the variant I bet on was not the one that passed.** I
predicted the 12%/14%/16% brakes on a three-month swing reading would land inside 15% at around
10-11% a year, with 14% the centre. The 14% one landed at 15.4% — just over — at only 9.3% a year.
The brake was costlier than M0001's exchange rate suggested: it cut 4.2 points of fall for 5.7
points of yearly return (about 1.4 points of return per point of fall, versus 0.8 on the old
momentum book). The 12% brake does pass every rule, but it beats SPY by 0.1 point a year, which
is a coin flip, not an edge.

**Did the expected failure happen? Yes, almost word for word.** I wrote that the binding fall
would be the August 1998 shock (Russia default / LTCM), that it would hit a calm book whose
three-month swing reading was still low, and that the 14% brake would land at 15-16%. It landed
at 15.4%, and in every single version the worst fall is the same stretch: end of June 1998 to end
of September 1998. The second-worst is always spring-summer 2006 (9-11%). 2000-02 and 2008 never
matter: the market trend gate already holds cash through them (those years show 0%).

**Why the one-month reading works.** The book only re-decides once a month. With a three-month
swing reading, the calm of April-June 1998 dominated the estimate at the end of July, so the book
went into August nearly as large as before. A one-month reading saw July's jumpiness alone and
cut the book before the worst of August. It also forgets a storm faster, so it re-invests sooner
afterwards: average invested share was 53% against 50% for the three-month version at the same
14% target. That is why it has both a smaller fall (14.1% vs 15.4%) and more return (10.8% vs
9.3%). It is better on both axes, not a trade of one for the other — which is what a real
mechanism looks like, rather than a dial turned.

**Worst year.** 2015, at −2.8% (the window ends in the middle of that year's correction). 1998,
the year of the worst fall, still ended +4.8% for the one-month version.

**Honest caveats.**
- The one-month version is one of five tries and its margin under the limit is 0.9 points. Some
  of that edge is surely selection. The lab's luck score already charges for that, and it says 0.90.
- 1998 is one event. The whole result rests on reacting to one shock better. The test window
  (2015-2026) has its own fast shocks (Aug 2015 tail, Feb 2018, Mar 2020, 2022) that would show
  whether this is real.
- The top-30 book was worse than top-20 here (16.2% fall), so "more names" is not a substitute
  for the faster reading.

**Comparison with near misses.** The old momentum book with the same kind of brake (M0001-TV12)
made 7.6% a year at a 12.9% fall — it failed to beat SPY. This one makes 10.8% at 14.1%. The
residual stock-picking hands the brake a better book to work with, which is exactly the argument
for this combination. Against the parent, the brake gave up 4.2 points of yearly return to remove
5.5 points of fall.

**My opinion:** this is the most promising result the lab has produced, and the direction deserves
more trials — but carefully, because the luck score is the only gate left and every new trial
raises it. The one-month version is the best-documented candidate yet: all four owner rules pass
on 20 years of history, and it beats its own three-month sibling on both return and fall for a
reason I can explain. I would not promote it today: 0.90 is not 0.95, and the lab's rules say
the bar is the bar. What I would try next is not more dials on this same brake (each one raises
the luck bar and the gains would be small) but one structural question: is the faster reading
the thing that matters? A brake keyed to an even quicker signal — the book's two-week swing, or
the market's own one-month swing — on the same top-20 residual book would tell us whether
"react within the month" is the lever, in one or two trials. If that also passes with a higher
luck score, that is the candidate to send to the test window.

methods.name: A faster crash gate for the residual-momentum book: the 1998-style shock, not the bear market
methods.hypothesis: Every trend-gated M0007 variant has its deepest drawdown in the three months after June 1998 (Russia/LTCM), not in 2000-02 or 2008, which the SPY 200-day gate turns flat (+0% in 2001, 2002 and 2008). Replacing the single 200-day gate on the raw-residual top-20 book with a two-speed gate - stay invested only while SPY is above both its 200-day and a short (50- or 100-day) average, or exit on a SPY drawdown-from-high trigger - should cut that one episode without giving back the long bull runs the 200-day gate captures. methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-06

## What we tried

The parent idea (M0002) braked the momentum strategy when its own day-to-day swings got unusually large. It beat the market but its worst fall stayed at 17.5-21.8%, over the 15% limit, because the big losses came in calm-looking markets. This method brakes on **the loss itself**: when the stocks we hold have fallen more than 8% from their best level of the last six months, we start selling down, reaching 25% invested by a 16% fall (one variant goes all the way to cash). The stock picks are the same top-20 momentum basket (F4-MOM12-N20-TREND) chosen once a month. Five variants re-check the brake weekly or daily on that monthly basket; one checks it only at the monthly re-pick.

## Results (1996 → Oct 2015, SPY with dividends: +7.9% a year)

| Variant | Yearly return | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unbraked parent basket (F4) | +16.2% | 22.2% | 2.27 | 1154 |
| Brake at -8%, checked monthly | +15.6% | 22.3% | 2.28 | 1155 |
| Brake at -8%, checked daily | +10.3% | 23.9% | 1.69 | 1449 |
| Brake at -8%, checked weekly (main bet) | +10.4% | 29.7% | 1.59 | 1387 |
| Brake at -6%, weekly | +9.5% | 27.7% | 1.58 | 1393 |
| Brake to cash, weekly | +9.9% | 32.9% | 1.58 | 1399 |
| Control: brake measured on new picks, weekly | +10.8% | 32.4% | 1.61 | 1387 |

All six beat SPY on return, and all six fail the 15% worst-fall limit, by 7 to 18 points. The best (monthly check, +15.6% a year) is essentially the unbraked basket: its DSR (the chance the edge is real after the lab's 100 tries) is 0.87, below the 0.95 bar. The worst year of the monthly variant is 2015 (-2.0%); the weekly main bet's worst year is 2011 (-8.9%).

## Why it failed

**The hypothesis failed, and backwards.** Checking more often made the worst fall *bigger*: 22% unbraked, 24% daily, 30% weekly. Two things happened.

1. **Whipsaw, worse than expected.** Momentum falls come as sharp V's (spring 2000, Aug 1998, May 2010, Aug 2011). The brake only engages after an 8% loss, so the first 8% of every fall is taken in full. It then sells near the bottom, and it only buys back once the basket has recovered half its fall. Spring 2000 shows it plainly: the weekly variant went from 3.57 to 2.74 (-23%) while the unbraked basket, holding through, was at a new high by August. Each V locks in a loss, and a string of them adds up to a deeper fall than just sitting still. Selling after a loss and buying after a gain is a cost in exactly the markets momentum lives in.
2. **The weekly check also re-checks the market's 200-day trend filter.** On a weekly re-scale the picker runs again, so if SPY dips under its 200-day average for a week the whole book is sold, and it is not bought back until the next monthly re-pick. That adds more sell-low/miss-the-rebound trips (late 2007, mid 2009 here). The control proves this matters: measuring the *new* picks (which by construction sit near their highs, so the brake should almost never fire) did just as badly as measuring the held book (32% vs 30%). So most of the damage in the weekly variants comes from the faster re-check machinery, not from the brake alone. I cannot separate the two from these trials; that is the next idea.

**The monthly check did nothing useful.** At a month start the held basket has usually either already rebounded or not yet fallen 8%: the 2006 unwind that sets the worst fall was a slow grind of small monthly losses (6.69 → 5.73 from March to August, about -14% month-end to month-end), which the brake never caught at a monthly check.

**Expected failure:** half right. Whipsaw happened and cost 5-6 points a year, more than the 2-4 I guessed, and the monthly variant did react too late. But I expected the worst fall to come down to 16-17%; instead it went up.

## Compared with the parent and near misses

M0002-REL-85 (12.6% a year, 18.4% worst fall) is clearly better than every variant here. M0007-N20-RAW (15.0%, 19.6%) remains the best return-per-fall in the lab. A drawdown brake on a single 20-stock basket is the wrong tool.

## My opinion:

Drop the "brake on losses" direction for the momentum book. A stop-loss on a momentum portfolio is a bet that falls keep going, and on this data they mostly snap back, so it pays the round trip every time. The one useful thing this run surfaced is a confound in the lab's own machinery: a weekly re-scale also re-runs the trend filter, so every "check risk weekly" result so far (here and M0004) mixes two effects. The next trial should be the plain monthly basket with a weekly re-scale and *no* brake, to price that machinery by itself; only then can any faster risk check be judged fairly. For actually reaching the 15% limit, I'd put effort into what we hold (residual momentum, more names) rather than when we hold it.
methods.verdict: Braking when our stocks fall 8% made things worse, not safer: checked weekly the worst fall grew from 22% to 30% and return dropped to about 10% a year, because momentum falls snap back and the brake sells near the bottom; checked monthly it barely fired.

methods.name: 52-week-high momentum: rank on nearness to the yearly high, not past return
methods.sourceRef: George & Hwang (2004), The 52-week high and momentum investing, J. Finance 59(5), doi:10.1111/j.1540-6261.2004.00695.x; Momentum crashes and the 52-week high, FAJ 2023
methods.hypothesis: Every momentum book in the lab ranks on 12-1 total or residual return, and its binding drawdowns (Mar-Aug 2006, Aug 1998, spring 2010/2011) are crowd unwinds of last year's big risers while SPY stays above its 200-day average. Nearness to the 52-week high captures most of momentum's return without its reversal, and momentum crashes concentrate in winners far below their highs. Ranking the top-20 by close / 252-day max close (ties by 12-1 return), with F4's screen, monthly rebalance and SPY 200-day gate, holds steadier names less exposed to speculative unwinds: max DD below F4's 22.2% at comparable CAGR, and the 50/50 blend with raw residual momentum below M0007-N20-RAW's 19.6%. Kill the direction if no variant gets max DD below 19.6%.
methods.expectedFailure: Nearness to the high is a low-volatility, late-cycle tilt: the names at their highs in a calm bull market are the same crowded quality/defensive leaders that sold off together in May 2006 and 2011, so the drawdown barely moves (19-22%) while CAGR drops 2-4 points because the pure nearness rank skips the strongest early-trend rebounders. Ties at nearness 1.0 in strong markets make the pure rank collapse into plain 12-1 momentum, so N20 looks like F4.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-06

## What we tried

Every momentum strategy in the lab picks the stocks that rose most over the past year. This one
picks the stocks trading **closest to their own highest price of the past year** (George & Hwang,
2004). The idea: a stock sitting at its high after a steady climb is a calmer holding than one
that doubled off a crash low, and the crowd unwinds that hurt momentum hit the second kind.
Everything else is the same as the lab's reference momentum book (F4-MOM12-N20-TREND): same
stock screen, rebalance once a month, equal weights, and all cash whenever SPY is below its
200-day average.

Four versions, fixed before the run:

| Version | What it holds | Yearly return (CAGR) | Worst fall | Gains vs losses (PF) | Trades | DSR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N20 | 20 stocks nearest their high | +8.0% | 18.0% | 1.53 | 2,670 | 0.61 |
| N30 | 30 stocks nearest their high | +8.3% | 17.3% | 1.61 | 3,604 | 0.74 |
| N20-BLEND | 20 stocks, half "near the high", half residual momentum | +9.7% | 16.8% | 1.54 | 2,162 | 0.70 |
| N30-BLEND | 30 stocks, same blend | +9.0% | **15.6%** | 1.64 | 2,863 | 0.72 |

SPY with dividends reinvested: **+7.9% a year** over the same 1996-2015 window.
For comparison, the lab's best so far, residual momentum (M0007-N20-RAW): +15.0% a year, worst fall 19.6%.

## Against the go-live rules

- **Beat SPY:** all four did, but the two pure versions only barely (+8.0% and +8.3% against +7.9%,
  about the same as just holding the index).
- **Worst fall at most 15%:** all four failed. The closest, N30-BLEND, lost 15.6% at its worst:
  0.6 points over the line. That is the nearest any method in the lab has come while also beating SPY
  on a fully stock-picking book, but over is over.
- **Gains vs losses at least 1.3 and 100+ trades:** all passed easily.
- **DSR at least 0.95:** all failed (0.61-0.74). DSR is the chance the result is real skill rather
  than luck, after allowing for the 94 strategies the lab has now tried. At 0.7 it is roughly a
  coin flip weighted slightly toward real; not good enough.

## When it hurt

On the month-end equity curve, every version's worst stretch is the same: the end of June to the
end of August 1998 (the Russian default / LTCM shock), while SPY was still above its 200-day
average, so the safety switch never fired. The worst calendar year for all four is 2015 (-6% for
the pure versions, -10% to -11% for the blends).

## Why

**The drawdown did shrink, as hoped.** Stocks near their highs are, by construction, ones that have
not fallen recently and are not the bounce-back rockets of a speculative rally. Every version came
in under residual momentum's 19.6% and well under the reference book's 22.2%.

**But the return went with it, far more than expected.** Looking year by year, the pure "near the
high" book made +14% in 1999 and -2% in 2000, where residual momentum made +56% and +21%; and
+16%/+33%/+5% in 2012-2014 against +33%/+47%/+18%. In strong, broad bull markets dozens of stocks
sit at or within a hair of their high, so the ranking becomes a near-random draw among quiet
large companies at their high rather than a pick of the strongest movers. The pick ends up close
to "an equal-weighted slice of the index that steps aside in bear markets", which is what its
+8% a year looks like. Blending in residual momentum brought back some of the bite (+9.7%) and
kept most of the safety.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- Hypothesis: "worst fall below 22.2% at comparable return". **Half held.** The worst fall dropped
  (15.6-18.0%), but the return was not comparable: 5-8 points a year lower than the parents.
- Expected failure: "the worst fall barely moves while return drops 2-4 points". **Wrong on the
  fall, too optimistic on the return.** The fall did move; the return dropped twice as much as feared.
- The kill rule ("kill if no version gets under 19.6%") was **not** triggered: all four did.

## My opinion:

"Nearness to the high" is a good **brake** and a bad **engine**. As the thing that picks stocks it
is too blunt: in good markets too many names tie at the top and the book loses the strong movers
that make momentum worth holding. But it clearly removes the stocks that cause the falls. So the
next step is to use it as a **filter, not a ranking**: keep residual momentum (the lab's best
engine) doing the picking, but only among stocks within, say, 10-20% of their yearly high. That
keeps M0007's +15% engine and throws away the far-below-high names the literature blames for
crashes. If that lands near 15% worst fall with 12%+ a year, it is the best shot the lab has. I
would not spend more trials on pure nearness ranks.
methods.verdict: Ranking on closeness to the yearly high cut the worst fall to 15.6-18.0% (best yet next to beating SPY) but dragged return down to +8.0-9.7% a year vs SPY's +7.9%: a good brake, a poor engine.

### 2026-10-07

### 2026-10-07

**The idea in one line.** Take the lab's best stock-picking book (buy the 20 stocks whose own rise,
after removing the market's move, was strongest over the past year; re-pick once a month) and put
an automatic safety exit under every stock: if a stock falls 15%, 20% or 25% below the price it
was bought near, sell it right away instead of waiting for next month's re-pick. In Gotrade this
is one Stop Sell order placed under each holding, which works with fractional shares.

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 104 trials at run time).** Rejected. Every
version still beats SPY by a wide margin, but the stops did not do their job.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| No brake, 15% stop | +950% | +12.6% | 18.6% | 1.76 | 1,723 | 0.87 | 0.68 | 0.86 | worst fall, luck score |
| No brake, 20% stop | +1,123% | +13.5% | 20.3% | 1.86 | 1,664 | 0.89 | 0.66 | 0.88 | worst fall, luck score |
| No brake, 25% stop | +1,296% | +14.3% | 20.7% | 2.00 | 1,633 | 0.92 | 0.69 | 0.90 | worst fall, luck score |
| Volatility brake + 20% stop | +546% | +9.9% | 12.5% | 1.79 | 1,657 | 0.89 | 0.79 | 0.87 | luck score |
| *Parent, no brake, no stop* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.94* | *0.77* | *0.91* | *worst fall* |
| *Parent, volatility brake, no stop* | *+660%* | *+10.8%* | *14.1%* | *2.03* | *1,588* | *0.93* | *0.76* | *0.90* | *luck score* |

SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the biggest
drop from a peak; the owner's limit is 15%. "Gains vs losses" (profit factor) is total profit on
winning trades divided by total loss on losing ones. The luck score (deflated Sharpe ratio) asks
how likely the result is real rather than the best of 104 lucky tries; the bar is 0.95.

**What happened.**
- On the book without a brake, the stops made the worst fall *bigger* at 20% and 25% (20.3% and
  20.7% vs 19.6%) and only 1 point smaller at 15% (18.6%), while costing 0.7 to 2.4 points of
  return a year. Gains vs losses dropped from 2.16 to 1.76–2.00: the stops turned many temporary
  dips into locked-in losses.
- On the braked book, the 20% stop did cut the worst fall from 14.1% to 12.5% and slightly
  improved return per unit of fall (0.79 vs 0.76), but cost 0.9 points of return a year and
  lowered the luck score (0.87 vs 0.90), so it moved further from eligibility, not closer.

**Why.** The worst falls of this book are not single stocks collapsing; they are the whole basket
falling together (the 1998 shock, the 2000–02 momentum crash, the 2009 rebound when beaten-down
stocks led). On those days many stops fire at once, often on gap-down opens below the stop price,
so the sale happens near the bottom. The book then holds cash until the next monthly re-pick and
misses the snap-back, and when it buys again the prices are higher. That is how a stop can make
the worst fall bigger: it turns a dip that would have recovered into a permanent loss, and the
re-entry starts from a lower equity. A single stock collapsing on its own news does happen, but
with 20 stocks at 5% each, one stock falling 40% costs the book only 2%, which is not what
decides the worst fall.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The hypothesis (a 20% stop lands the unbraked book near
15–16% worst fall at about +13% a year) failed: the worst fall rose to 20.3%. The expected
failure (stops fire together in basket-wide falls, sell near the bottom and miss the rebound)
is what happened, almost word for word. It agrees with the basket-brake method from yesterday
(sold at the bottom of rebounds) and with the old observation that a stop-loss on momentum sells
at the bottom of the bounce.

**Comparison.** The volatility brake (reduce how much is held when the basket has been swinging
hard) remains the only risk control the lab has found that cuts this book's worst fall cheaply,
because it acts before and during calm-to-stormy transitions rather than after a stock has already
fallen. Per-stock stops act after the fact.

**For the owner's question (can a hold-for-months method carry an automatic safety exit?).**
Mechanically yes, but on the evidence it should not: on this book a resting Stop Sell under each
stock lowers return and does not lower the worst fall. A braked book with a 20% stop is a
legitimate, executable version (all four owner rules pass: beats SPY, 12.5% worst fall, 1.79
gains vs losses, 1,657 trades), but it is strictly worse than the same book without the stop on
the one bar it fails (luck score).

My opinion: per-stock stops on momentum are a dead end; I would not spend more trials on stop
widths, trailing stops or ATR-based stops for this book, because the mechanism (basket-wide falls,
sell at the bottom, miss the rebound) applies to all of them. The one variant worth a single try
is fixing the re-entry, not the stop: let a stopped-out stock be bought back at the next weekly
check if it is still in the top 20, so a stop costs a week of the rebound instead of a month.
Beyond that, the lab's binding constraint is now the luck score on books that already pass every
owner rule, and more variants of the same book make that bar harder, not easier. The better use
of trials is a genuinely different source of return that could stand on its own.
methods.verdict: A safety exit under each stock made things worse: the worst fall did not shrink (18.6-20.7% vs 19.6%) and return dropped 0.7-2.4 points a year, because the stops fire together in market-wide falls, sell near the bottom and miss the rebound.

### 2026-10-07

**The idea in one line.** Yesterday's test (M0019) showed that a safety exit under each stock
hurts the best stock-picking book, because a stock sold in a market-wide dip waited up to a month
in cash and missed the bounce. This test lets that stock come back at the next weekly check, as
long as it is still in this month's list, so a safety exit costs at most a week of the bounce.

**How it was set up.** The book still picks its 20 stocks once a month (the stocks whose own rise,
after removing the market's move, was strongest over the past year). Every week it re-issues that
same list at fresh prices: a stock sold by its safety exit since the last check is bought back,
with a new exit 20% below its latest price. Checking weekly also nudges every holding back toward
an equal share each week, so one version runs the weekly checks with no safety exit at all, to
show what the weekly checking costs on its own. (Assumption, written down before the run: the new
month's list is first issued at the first weekly check of the month, up to a few trading days
after the monthly parent buys it.)

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 107 trials at run time).** Rejected.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |

| Weekly checks, 20% exit, buy back | +1,274% | +14.2% | 18.9% | 1.86 | 1,744 | 0.89 | 0.75 | 0.88 | worst fall, luck score |
| Braked book, 20% exit, buy back | +553% | +9.9% | 16.2% | 1.76 | 1,737 | 0.87 | 0.61 | 0.85 | worst fall, luck score |
| *Monthly parent, no exit* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.94* | *0.77* | *0.91* | *worst fall* |
| *M0019: monthly, 20% exit, no buy back* | *+1,123%* | *+13.5%* | *20.3%* | *1.86* | *1,664* | *0.89* | *0.66* | *0.88* | *worst fall* |
| *Braked parent, no exit (M0011's best)* | *+660%* | *+10.8%* | *14.1%* | *2.03* | *1,588* | *0.93* | *0.76* | *0.90* | *luck score* |

SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the biggest
drop from a peak (the limit is 15%); "gains vs losses" is profit on winners over loss on losers;
the luck score asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of 107 lucky tries (the bar
is 0.95).

**What happened.**
- Checking weekly costs nothing by itself. The control matched the monthly parent almost exactly
  (+15.3% vs +15.0% a year, worst fall 19.3% vs 19.6%, same luck score). Nudging holdings back to
  equal shares every week neither helped nor hurt.
- Buying back did repair part of the damage from yesterday: against M0019's exit with no buy-back,
  return rose from +13.5% to +14.2% a year and the worst fall fell from 20.3% to 18.9%.
- But against its own control the safety exit still loses: 1.1 points of return a year, gains vs
  losses down from 2.11 to 1.86, luck score down from 0.91 to 0.88, for a worst fall only 0.4
  points smaller (19.3% to 18.9%), still far over 15%.
- On the braked book it was worse than useless: the worst fall rose from 14.1% to 16.2%, so the
  version that passed every owner rule no longer does.

**Why.** Exactly the expected failure. The big falls of this book are the whole market falling for
weeks, not a few days. A stock sold on a gap-down is bought back a week later while the fall is
still going, and is often sold again lower: 124 extra trades on the unbraked book, each a small
loss plus costs. On the braked book there is a second effect: the brake had already cut how much
is held, and buying stopped stocks back at the start-of-month share undoes part of that cut in the
middle of a fall, which is how its worst fall got bigger.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The pre-stated test was: if buying back does not bring the
worst fall under the parent's 19.6% at a similar return, per-stock exits are closed for this
family. The worst fall did land under 19.6% (18.9%), but return fell by 0.8 points against the
parent and 1.1 against the like-for-like control, and the luck score fell, so the result is not
"similar return". The expected failure (bought back into a falling basket, stopped again, more
trades, worse gains vs losses) is what happened.

My opinion: per-stock safety exits are closed for this book. Two careful tries with opposite
fixes both found the same thing: the exits fire in market-wide falls, and no re-entry timing
recovers what they give up. The braked book's volatility brake remains the only risk control that
works here, because it cuts how much is held before and during the storm instead of selling single
stocks after they have fallen. The useful by-product is that weekly checking is free for this
book, which matters if a future idea needs a weekly signal. The next trials should look for a
second, different source of return to combine with this book, not another way to protect it.
methods.verdict: Buying a stopped stock back at the next weekly check recovered part of what the safety exit lost, but it still trailed the same book without exits (14.2% vs 15.3% a year, worst fall 18.9% vs 19.3%) and made the braked book's worst fall worse (16.2% vs 14.1%): per-stock exits are closed for this book.
