### 2026-10-07

### 2026-10-07

**The idea in one line.** RM (the braked momentum book now on paper) decides once a month how much
of its money to hold, based on how wildly its 20 stocks swung over the past month. This test reads
that same brake every week instead, while still picking the 20 stocks only once a month. The owner
said a weekly check is fine if it performs better.

**Why it could work this time.** An earlier test (M0004) read a three-month swing measure weekly on
the plain momentum book and found it added cost and nothing else: a three-month measure barely
changes from one week to the next. RM's brake reads only the last month, which can change a lot
within a month, so a weekly re-read carries new information. The test before this one (M0020)
had also shown that checking this book weekly costs nothing by itself.

**Result (dev window 1996-01-03 → 2015-10-16, N = 110 trials at run time).** Rejected, but the two
main versions are the lab's best results so far: they pass every one of the owner's rules and
miss only the luck score.

| Version | Total return | Per year | Worst fall | Gains vs losses | Trades | Sharpe | Return per unit of fall | Luck score | Missed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **Weekly brake, 14% swing limit** | **+633%** | **+10.6%** | **12.4%** | **2.04** | 1,592 | 0.94 | **0.86** | **0.912** | luck score |
| **Weekly brake, 16% swing limit** | **+789%** | **+11.7%** | **14.3%** | **2.06** | 1,589 | **0.95** | 0.82 | **0.916** | luck score |
| Weekly brake + weekly market filter | +384% | +8.3% | 15.6% | 1.64 | 1,761 | 0.79 | 0.53 | 0.765 | worst fall, luck score |
| *RM today: monthly brake, 14% limit* | *+660%* | *+10.8%* | *14.1%* | *2.03* | *1,588* | *0.93* | *0.76* | *0.897 (N=90)* | *luck score* |
| *Same book, no brake* | *+1,502%* | *+15.0%* | *19.6%* | *2.16* | *1,596* | *0.94* | *0.77* | *0.914 (N=85)* | *worst fall* |

SPY with dividends returned +351% over the same window (7.9% a year). "Worst fall" is the biggest
drop from a peak (the owner's limit is 15%); "gains vs losses" is profit on winners over loss on
losers (limit 1.3); "return per unit of fall" (MAR) is yearly return divided by the worst fall; the
luck score (deflated Sharpe ratio) asks how likely the result is real rather than the best of 110
tries (the bar is 0.95).

**What happened.**
- With the same 14% limit as RM, reading the brake weekly cut the worst fall from 14.1% to 12.4%
  while giving up only 0.2 points of return a year (10.6% vs 10.8%). Return per unit of fall rose
  from 0.76 to 0.86, the best in the lab.
- That extra safety leaves room for more exposure: at a 16% limit the worst fall is 14.3% (still
  under 15%) and return rises to 11.7% a year, with the lab's highest Sharpe (0.95, steadiness of
  the gains) and highest luck score (0.916).
- Re-reading the market filter weekly as well was a clear mistake: it sold on dips and stayed in
  cash until the month ended, missing the rebound (worst fall 15.6%, return 8.3%, gains vs losses
  1.64). This is the same whipsaw the lab journal recorded for the basket brake.
- The luck score rose (RM's 0.897 at 90 tries to 0.912–0.916 at 110 tries), even though the bar
  for it rose with 20 more tries. It is still short of 0.95.

**Why.** A fast shock that starts in the middle of a month met RM at full strength, because RM only
checks its brake at the month's start. With a weekly check the brake sees the swings growing within
days and cuts how much is held before most of the fall, then lets exposure back as the swings calm,
without changing which stocks are held. That is different from every failed control in this
family: stops, basket brakes and a weekly market filter all sell after prices have already fallen
and then sit out the rebound. The weekly brake trims gradually, keeps the same stocks, and adds
back gradually.

**Hypothesis vs expected failure.** The hypothesis held on the worst fall and the return: at 14%
it predicted about 11–12% worst fall at a similar return (got 12.4% at 10.6%), and at 16% a worst
fall near 14% with return toward 12% a year (got 14.3% at 11.7%). It did not reach a luck score of
0.95 (got 0.916). The expected failure (the brake lags the crash and the extra trades cost more
than the fall saved) did not happen for the brake alone: only 4 more trades than RM in 20 years.
It did happen, as predicted, for the weekly market filter.

**For the owner.** This book is executable: it picks 20 stocks once a month (as RM does) and once a
week may trim or top up all holdings by the same proportion, as fractional limit orders in Gotrade.
The nightly paper engine cannot run a weekly-adjust rule yet; a handover for that feature was
written today (docs/handover/2026-10-07-paper-split-cadence.md).

My opinion: this is the strongest direction the lab has. A weekly brake is strictly better than
RM's monthly one on everything that matters here (smaller fall, same return at 14%; more return
inside the limit at 16%), and the mechanism makes sense rather than being a lucky setting. I would
not spend more trials tuning the swing limit or the reading length: each one raises the luck bar,
and the improvement came from the weekly re-read, not from the setting. Once paper trading can run
a weekly-adjust rule, the 16% version should replace RM on paper (owner's decision, as RM was): it
passes every owner rule with more room than RM and has the best luck score in the lab. The next
lab trials should combine this book with a second, different source of return (the calm-stock
blend already queued), with the weekly brake on top, because a steadier combined curve is the
most direct way to lift the luck score past 0.95.

insights.title: Volatility scaling buys drawdown at a near-linear price in return
insights.body: Scaling top-20 momentum to a 10-12% own-volatility target cut max DD from 22% to 11-13% but also CAGR from 16% to 6-7.6%, because a ~22%-vol book is held at about half exposure all the time, not just in crashes. insights.title: FND, a company-fundamentals picker, now trades on paper, and paper is its real test
insights.body:
Most strategies Sera has tried pick stocks by how their price has moved. This one is different: each month it picks the 20 big US companies whose own reports look best. It favours companies that are cheap next to what they own, earn well on their money, make healthy profits on what they sell, and recently beat what was expected of their earnings. Those four signals have a long track record in finance research.

**Why it went to paper even though the history test marked it "rejected".** The company reports Sera can read only start in 2015. The history test runs from 1996 to 2015, so for 19 of those 20 years the strategy had nothing to go on and just sat in cash. That's why it "failed": it never really got to play. The idea wasn't proven wrong. It was never tested.

Waiting is the only fair test left. From here on, FND trades every night with pretend money, its rules are locked, and nothing before its first night counts. That's also why it isn't a candidate for real money: it hasn't earned it yet.

**What to watch:** month by month, does it keep up with or beat SPY, and how far does it fall in a bad month? A few good months could be luck. A year of steady results would mean something.

insights.title: A slow signal does not get better by checking it more often
insights.body:
The lab has a stock picker that cuts its own exposure when the market gets choppy. It measures choppiness over the past three months. We wondered whether checking that measure weekly instead of monthly would catch crashes faster, so we built the ability to pick stocks on one schedule and set exposure on another, and tried every combination.

Checking weekly did not help. It made things slightly worse. The reason is simple once you see it: a three-month average barely moves in a week. Reading it every Monday gives back almost the same number it gave a month ago, so the faster schedule learns nothing new. What it does do is create four times as many chances to shuffle the book around that same unchanged number, and each shuffle costs a little. The worst fall improved by less than one point, from 11.0 percent to 10.3 percent, while yearly growth dropped from 6.1 percent to 4.8 percent. We paid more than we got.

The cleanest proof sits in the version with the market-trend filter switched off. Measured monthly and measured weekly, it scored identically. With nothing else in front of it, re-reading the choppiness number weekly changed literally nothing.

The useful lesson is a rule of thumb for everything the lab builds next. How often it is worth re-checking something is decided by how fast that something actually moves, not by how often we are willing to trade. Pair a three-month measure with a monthly schedule. If we want a genuinely faster reaction, we need a measure that genuinely moves faster, such as one built from the last few weeks rather than the last few months.

One thing did come out of it worth keeping. Splitting the two schedules let us settle an old question: the heavy trading in the weekly version came almost entirely from re-choosing which stocks to hold, not from adjusting how much to hold. Re-choosing costs about eight times as much trading as re-sizing. That is now a measured fact rather than a guess.

insights.title: Spreading money more cleverly is not the same as holding less of it
insights.body: We took the stock picker that buys the twenty strongest risers and, instead of splitting the money evenly between them, worked out from a year of daily prices which mix of those same twenty moves around the least, and bought that mix. It worked as mathematics and failed as safety. The month-to-month wobble of the account dropped by about a fifth. The worst fall, which is the thing the owner actually cares about and the thing our rules measure, dropped from 22.2% to 21.6% - almost nothing - while the yearly rate of return fell from 16.2% to 13.7%. We paid two and a half points of return for half a point of safety. The lesson is that wobble and worst fall are two different risks and a clever split only touches the first one. An ordinary month is made of twenty stocks disagreeing with each other, and a clever split smooths that out. A bad month is made of twenty stocks all falling together, and then there is no clever split, because they were all the same bet to begin with. The proof is the version we ran with the safety switch turned off: it fell 54% at its worst and lost 41% in 2008, slightly worse than just owning the market through the crash. The earlier method that simply held half its money in cash fell 18% in the same test. Holding less protects you. Holding the same amount, arranged more intelligently, does not. What to do about it: stop trying weighting schemes inside a single-theme book. Risk parity and its cousins would hit the same wall for the same reason. Safety in this kind of portfolio has to come from owning less of it at the right moments, or from owning something genuinely different, not from rearranging the same bet.

insights.title: The crash that keeps blocking us is 2006, and our safety switch never saw it
insights.body: Every version of the strongest-risers picker that uses the market safety switch - hold stocks while the market is above its 200-day average, otherwise sit in cash - has its worst moment in the same five months: March to August 2006. Not the dot-com bust, not 2008. In those five months the market itself fell at worst 7.6% and never once dipped below its 200-day average, so the safety switch stayed in the on position the entire time and the book rode it all the way down, losing about 18%. What crashed in 2006 was not the market. It was the theme: the energy, materials and emerging-market names that had all climbed smoothly for a year unwound together in May. This matters because it reframes the problem. We have been trying to make the book safer in general, when what actually blocks us is one specific kind of event that our one safety switch is blind to by construction - a crash in what we own while the market around it is fine. Worse, the clever-split experiment made 2006 worse rather than better, because the optimiser leans toward whatever has been calmest over the past year, and in 2006 the calmest names were exactly the smooth one-way climbers that broke hardest. A year of quiet upward drift looks like safety to the arithmetic and is in truth a crowded trade. What to do about it: give the book a second safety switch that watches the book itself rather than the market. When the account is more than some distance below its own previous high, cut back until it recovers. That is pointed straight at the event that keeps stopping us, and unlike holding permanent cash it costs nothing in the calm years. It is queued as the next trial.

insights.title: Taking the market's move out of a stock's score is the cheapest safety we have bought so far
insights.body:
Until now, every way we found to make the strategy fall less has cost about as much return as it saved. Shrinking positions when markets get jumpy cut the worst fall from 22% to 13%, and it cut the yearly return from 16% to 8% doing it - roughly one point of return for one point of safety.

The market-adjusted picker is the first exception. Before ranking stocks on how much they rose over the past year, it subtracts the part of each rise that the whole market explains, and ranks on what is left - the company's own story. It stays just as fully invested as before, buys the same number of names, and still turned a 22.2% worst fall into a 19.6% one while giving up only 1.2 points of yearly return. That is about half price.

Why it works: a stock that rose mostly because the market rose is a bet on the market, not on the company. A book full of those bets is a leveraged market bet in disguise, and it falls hardest exactly when the market turns. Removing that part of the score leaves a book of genuine company winners that does not all move together.

What to do about it: this is a better starting point, not a finished strategy, because 19.6% is still well over the 15% limit. The right next move is to put our existing position-shrinking overlay on top of this better book rather than on the old one - we would be spending a 15% yearly return down to about 11% instead of spending a 16% one down to 8%. That is the first combination where the arithmetic reaches the limit with something left over for the owner.

insights.title: A buy-only strategy's crash is the market's crash, so a cleverer stock score cannot prevent it
insights.body:
The research papers behind this experiment report that market-adjusted momentum largely cures the sudden collapses that plague momentum strategies. We tested that claim directly by removing our market-trend safety switch and letting the stock score fend for itself. It fell 51% from its peak and lost 34% in 2008 - no better than the plain version.

The reason is a mismatch we should remember. Those papers study a portfolio that buys winners and sells losers short at the same time. Its collapses really are a momentum-specific event: after a bad market the losers it is short are the jumpy, high-market-sensitivity names, and when the market rebounds those explode upward and the short side blows up. We never sell short. We only buy. So our collapses are simply the market's collapses, arriving through the stocks we hold, and no improvement to how we choose stocks can remove them.

What to do about it: keep treating the market-trend switch - being in cash when the market is below its long-term average - as the one thing that controls our worst falls, and treat every stock-scoring idea as a way to earn more while invested, never as a substitute for it. Also, when a paper promises crash protection, check first whether it is protecting the short side we do not have. Usefully, the test also showed where our remaining risk actually sits: with the switch on, 2001, 2002 and 2008 were all flat, and the deepest fall of the whole twenty years came from one fast shock in the autumn of 1998 that the switch reacted to too late.

insights.title: The falls that hurt this strategy happen in calm markets, not crashes
insights.body:
A momentum strategy that buys the twenty strongest stocks and sits in cash when the market is below its 200-day average has almost no bad years. Over 1996-2015 its worst calendar year was about minus three percent, and 2001, 2002 and 2008 came out flat, because it was in cash through those crashes.

Its losses come from somewhere else entirely. The four worst spells were March to August 2006, the summer of 1998, the spring of 2010 and the autumn of 2011. In every one of them the market was fine and the particular stocks the strategy had crowded into reversed. Spring 2006 is the clearest: commodity and emerging-market names had run hard, the market stayed comfortably above its 200-day average so the cash switch never tripped, and the holdings unwound anyway.

This matters because the usual safety device is a brake tied to how much the holdings have been bouncing around lately. That brake cannot help here. The jump in bounciness and the loss are the same event, and a three-month measurement needs weeks to notice it, so the brake comes on after the money is gone. It protected against long bad stretches, which is real, and did nothing about sharp ones.

What to do about it: stop trying to predict these falls from past bounciness and react to the fall itself. A brake that watches whether the stocks currently held are below their own recent high can move on day one of a reversal instead of six weeks in. That is the next thing worth testing.

insights.title: Turning a strategy down is not the same as making it safer, and the lab keeps proving it
insights.body:
The lab has now run three versions of the same experiment: take the strongest stock picker it has, and shrink how much money it puts to work when things look risky. The unshrunk picker grew 16.2 percent a year and fell 22.2 percent at its worst. Shrinking it all the time gave 7.6 percent and 12.9 percent. Shrinking it only when the holdings were unusually jumpy gave 12.6 percent and 18.4 percent.

Line those up against how much money each one actually kept in stocks on an average day, and the picture is stark. Every single version gave up roughly the same amount of fall for each unit of money it put at work: around thirty-five, in those units, whether it braked hard, softly, cleverly, or not at all. The brake was not removing risk. It was turning the whole thing down, and return and risk came down together in step.

The one real gain is smaller and worth keeping: braking only when the holdings are jumpy for themselves earns more per unit of money at work than braking all the time, about 24 against 21 in the same units. A well-aimed brake is better than a permanent one. It is just a refinement on a dial, not an escape from it.

The risk this creates for the lab is spending run after run on that dial. Because the trade is so close to a straight line, where any setting lands can now be read off in advance, and the honest answer is that no setting of it produces a strategy that is better rather than smaller. The remaining problem is the quality of the stock picking itself, not what is done with the picks afterwards.

insights.title: The lab's own searching is raising the bar it has to clear
insights.body:
Before any strategy is allowed near real money, the lab asks how likely its result is to be genuine rather than the best of many lucky tries. The more things have been tried, the better a result has to be. That count has now reached eighty-five, and the bar has moved with it.

Working from where this run landed, a strategy of this shape now needs a reward-per-unit-of-wobble score of about one a year to clear the bar. The best this lab has ever recorded is 0.89, from the plain momentum picker with no brake on it. This run's best was 0.87. Everything tried so far sits just under the line, and roughly every seventy further trials pushes the line a little further away.

The important part is where that score does not come from. Across this whole family of experiments the score barely moved: 0.89 with no brake, 0.81 braked all the time, 0.87 braked only in jumpy spells. Adjusting how much money is at work changes the return and the swings together and leaves their ratio alone. So no amount of further work on brakes, targets or triggers will clear this bar.

What will clear it is picking better stocks: a signal that earns more for the risk it takes. That points the next runs at the queued work on momentum measured against what the market did anyway, and on weighting holdings by how they move together rather than equally. It also argues for being sparing with trials, because every one spent raises the bar for the ones after it.

insights.title: Sera 20261006-1137: three ways to make a winner safe, and only changing what we buy worked
insights.body:
Three sessions ran side by side, each trying a different way to make the same winning
strategy safe enough to use. The strategy is the one that keeps coming back: buy the twenty
stocks that rose most over the past year, refresh the list monthly, and sit in cash whenever
the market itself is below its long-run average. It makes about 16% a year against the
market's 8%. It has one flaw, and the whole lab is now organised around that flaw: at its
worst it fell 22% from a peak, and our limit is 15%.

There are only three places you can intervene. You can change how much you hold and when
(braking). You can change how the money is split between the names you hold (weighting). Or
you can change which names you pick in the first place (the score). This batch tried one of
each, deliberately, so that a failure would tell us something a success could not.

**Braking and weighting both failed, and failed for the same reason.** The first session
braked only when the basket itself turned jumpy, leaving it fully invested in calm spells.
The second kept the same twenty names and the same full investment, but worked out from the
past year of prices which mix of them moves together least, and held that mix instead of
equal amounts. Both beat the market comfortably. Neither got the worst fall below 17%.

The second session produced the cleanest evidence of the batch. Its clever splitting did
exactly what it promised: the day-to-day wobble dropped by almost a fifth, with every penny
still invested. The worst fall barely moved, from 22% to 21.6%. **Wobble and worst fall are
not the same risk**, and we have now paid to learn that in the only way that counts. The
first session found the matching fact from the other side: across all nine braked versions
we have ever run, the worst fall shrinks in exact proportion to how much you were holding.
Turning the strategy down does not make it safer. It just makes it smaller, and the return
goes down by the same proportion.

**Both sessions then independently found the same culprit, which nobody was looking for.**
The falls that block us are not the crashes. 2001, 2002 and 2008 are quiet in these results,
because the market was below its average and we were in cash, exactly as designed. The damage
is done in March to August 2006, in August 1998, and in the spring of 2010 and 2011 — stretches
where the market was calm, above its average, never triggered our safety switch, and our basket
of recent winners fell apart anyway. In 2006 the market fell at most 8% and never broke its
average, while the basket lost about 18%. These are not market crashes. They are the crowd
getting out of last year's winners all at once. **Our one safety switch watches the market, and
this risk is not in the market.** That is the single most useful thing this batch found.

**The third session is the one that worked, and it worked by changing the score.** Instead of
ranking stocks on how much they rose, it ranked them on how much they rose *after taking out
the part the whole market explains* — the stock's own story, with the market's tide removed.
Nothing else changed: same number of names, same monthly refresh, same safety switch, same
full investment. It returned 15% a year against the market's 8% at a worst fall of 19.6%, and
that is the best return-per-unit-of-fall this lab has ever recorded, in a brand new family
that went straight to the top on its first attempt. It is still 4.6 points outside the limit,
so it is not usable. But it is the only thing in three batches that improved the trade-off
rather than sliding along it. One footnote worth keeping: the textbook refinement of this
idea, which rescales each stock's score by how erratic it is, made things worse every time.
The plain version won.

**So: changing what we buy is alive. Changing how much we hold, or how we split it, is dead.**
We should stop spending runs on risk overlays. Three batches have now established that they
move the strategy along a fixed line rather than lifting it off that line.

**A new obstacle has appeared, and it is one we create ourselves.** Every result is discounted
for how many things we have tried — 85 experiments now — because the more ideas you test, the
likelier it is that the best one is luck. We are close to the point where the remaining gap is
this discount rather than the drawdown. On this batch's evidence it needs a strategy whose
quality score reaches about 1.0; the market-adjusted scorer reached 0.94, the best we have ever
had and better than the 0.89 one session believed was our ceiling. It is reachable, but only
by a genuinely better score. No amount of risk management will get there, because risk
management does not move that number at all. **The honest reading is that our own searching is
raising the bar we have to clear, and only better ideas, not better safety nets, can clear it.**

**What would unlock the most.** We do not need new data to attack the real obstacle; we need a
second safety switch that watches our own basket instead of the market. Both failing sessions
converged on the same design without talking to each other: brake when the basket itself is
down from its own recent peak, rather than when it looks jumpy. The reason braking on jumpiness
fails is now understood — jumpiness arrives *with* the fall, not before it, so the brake is
still off while the loss is being made. A basket's distance below its own high is visible
immediately. Beyond that, the thing we genuinely lack is any direct measure of how crowded a
trade has become, which is what actually causes these unwinds; nothing in our data sees it.

**What the next batch should try.** First, the market-adjusted scorer combined with modest
braking — this is the one combination whose arithmetic plausibly closes, because it starts from
a better trade-off than anything else we have, and the braking line it would slide down crosses
our limit while still beating the market. Second, the own-basket brake, which two sessions
recommended independently and which attacks the 2006-style unwind directly. Third, one cheap
run holding 30, 40 and 50 names instead of 20: simply holding more names has cut the worst fall
from 33% to 20% as we widened from 5 to 20, and we have never looked past 20. Spreading wider
may be a better brake than any of our clever ones, and it costs one run to find out.

No test-window look was spent this batch. Our one chance to check against unseen data is still
untouched, which is right, because nothing yet deserves it.

insights.title: A stop-loss on a momentum strategy sells at the bottom of the bounce
insights.body: We tried cutting back the stock-picking strategy whenever the stocks it held had fallen 8% from their recent best, getting down to a quarter invested by a 16% fall. It made things worse. Checked every week, the worst fall grew from 22% to 30%, and yearly return dropped from about 16% to about 10%. The reason is that the falls in these winning stocks are usually sharp dips that recover within weeks: the brake sold after the damage was done and bought back only after half the recovery had already happened, locking in a loss every time. Lesson: for this kind of strategy, reacting to losses after they happen is a cost, not a protection. Safety has to come from what we hold, not from when we run away.

insights.title: Checking risk weekly quietly re-runs the market switch too
insights.body: When a strategy keeps its monthly stock picks but adjusts how much it holds every week, the weekly check also re-asks whether the market is above its long-term average. If the market dips below for a single week, everything is sold and not bought back until the next month. That adds extra sell-low trips we never meant to test. A control test in this run that should have done almost nothing did just as badly as the real brake, which points at this hidden effect. Every 'check risk weekly' result so far mixes the two, so we should measure the weekly check by itself before trusting any of them.

insights.title: A safety brake that looks at last month, not last quarter, finally kept a winning strategy inside the limit
insights.body: We took the best stock-picking strategy we have and added a brake: when its stocks have been swinging hard, it holds less of them and keeps the rest in cash. With the brake judging the swings over the past three months, the strategy still fell 15.4% at its worst, just over the 15% limit. Judging them over only the past month, the worst fall dropped to 14.1% and the yearly return went up, from 9.3% to 10.8% (SPY made 7.9%). The reason is timing. The fall that always hurts is the sudden 1998 shock, which came after a calm spring. A three-month reading still remembered the calm and kept the strategy fully loaded; a one-month reading saw the jitters of July and cut back before August. It also relaxes faster after a storm, so the money gets back to work sooner. This is the first strategy in the lab to pass all four of the owner's rules on 20 years of history. It is not promoted yet, because the lab's own luck check (how likely this is real after 90 tries) reads 0.90, not the 0.95 it needs.

insights.title: Stocks near their yearly high fall less, but they also stop the strategy from earning
insights.body: We tried picking the stocks trading closest to their highest price of the past year, instead of the ones that rose most. The worst fall shrank (to between 15.6% and 18%, against about 20% for our best stock-picker), which supports the idea that crashes come from stocks that bounced up from far below their high. But yearly return fell from about 15% to 8-10%, barely above simply holding the S&P 500's 7.9%. In strong markets dozens of stocks sit right at their high, so ranking on it stops telling strong stocks from merely steady ones. The lesson: closeness to the high is better used to rule stocks out than to pick them. Next we keep the best picker and only let it choose among stocks near their high.

insights.title: Every new try makes the next winner harder to trust
insights.body: The best result so far missed only one bar: the luck check, which asks whether a result could simply be the best of many attempts. Each experiment the lab runs raises that bar a little, because more tries mean more chances to get lucky. So the way to pass is not to keep turning dials on the same strategy, which adds tries and gains little, but to test one clear question at a time with as few versions as possible. Future experiments on this strategy should use one or two versions, not five.

insights.title: Sera 20261006-2027: the first all-rules pass, held back only by the luck test
insights.body:
This batch tried the three ideas the last batch asked for, and for the first time one strategy
passed every rule the owner set on the twenty years of history we test on. It is not usable yet,
and the reason is now the most important thing to understand about this lab.

**The one that worked.** Start from the best stock picker we had: each month, buy the twenty
stocks whose rise over the past year owes the most to their own story rather than to the market
lifting everything, and sit in cash when the market is below its long-run average. On its own it
made 15% a year but fell 19.6% at its worst, past our 15% limit. This session added a brake: when
the basket has been swinging wildly over the past month, hold less of it. Every earlier brake we
tried looked at the last three months and reacted too late, after the damage was done. Looking at
only the last month reacts in time. The result: 10.8% a year against the market's 7.9%, a worst
fall of 14.1%, gains about twice the size of losses, and nearly 1,600 trades. That clears the
return rule, the fall rule, the gains-to-losses rule and the enough-trades rule, all at once.
A gentler setting of the same brake passed too, but beat the market by only a hair.

**Why it still is not allowed near money.** Before anything is promoted, the lab asks how likely
it is that a result this good is the luckiest of all the things we have tried, rather than a
real edge. We have now tried a hundred variations. Against that count, this strategy scores 0.90
on a scale where we require 0.95. It is close, and it is the closest thing to a genuine pass we
have ever had, but the rule exists precisely so that we do not fool ourselves on the hundredth try.
Every further experiment raises that bar a little more, so each next run has to be chosen for
what it can teach, not fired off in hope.

**The brake on our own losses made things worse.** The second session cut back whenever the stocks
it held fell 8%. Two sessions last batch had recommended exactly this, and it failed badly. Checked
every week, the worst fall grew from 22% to 30%. The reason is that dips in this kind of strategy
usually snap back within days: the brake sold near the bottom, missed the rebound, then bought
back higher. Checked every month, it hardly ever fired. Selling because you are down is the
classic stop-loss, and on a strategy built on trends that recover, it sells at the worst moment.

**Stocks near their yearly high are calmer but earn less.** The third session tried a different way
of choosing stocks altogether, picking the ones trading closest to their highest price of the past
year, an idea from a well-known 2004 finance paper. It was a genuinely good brake: the worst fall
dropped to 15.6%, barely over the limit, without holding any cash. But the return dropped to
roughly what the market makes, so there was nothing left to show for the extra safety. Good at
falling less, poor at making money.

**What looks alive.** Picking stocks on their own story, with the market's tide removed, is now
clearly our best engine, and a fast one-month brake is the first brake that has ever paid its way.
Together they made the lab's first all-rules pass. "Near the yearly high" is useful as a filter on
which stocks to consider, even though it is a poor way to choose among them.

**What looks dead.** Stop-loss style braking on our own losses. Slow, three-month volatility
brakes. Re-checking risk every week, which also turned out to re-run the market-trend switch more
often than intended and caused extra whipsaw.

**What would unlock the most.** Nothing new in data this time. The obstacle is the luck test, and
only two things move it: a stronger result, or fewer wasted tries. More history would help most of
all, because a longer track record makes any real edge easier to tell apart from luck.

**What the next batch should try.** First, the winning combination with a still faster brake,
reading the last two weeks instead of the last month, to see whether reacting sooner lifts return
without giving back safety. Second, the market-adjusted picker restricted to stocks near their
yearly high, so the calm-stocks filter supplies the safety and the strong picker supplies the
return. Third, rather than adding more variations of the same picker, look for a genuinely
different source of return that could be blended with it, because two independent edges score
better on the luck test than one edge tuned many times.

No look at the held-back test years was spent. Nothing qualified, because the luck test blocked
the one strategy that passed everything else, which is exactly what that test is for.

insights.title: An automatic sell order under each stock hurts a hold-for-months momentum strategy
insights.body: We gave the best stock-picking book a safety exit: sell any stock that falls 15%, 20% or 25% below what we paid. It made the worst fall no smaller (and at 20% and 25%, slightly bigger) and cost up to 2.4 points of return a year. The reason is that this book's big falls are the whole market falling together, not one stock collapsing. On those days many safety exits fire at once, often at a gap-down opening price, so the selling happens near the bottom, and the money sits in cash until next month's re-pick while prices bounce back. One stock collapsing on its own costs the book little, because each stock is only 5% of the money. For the owner: for the monthly methods, a resting Stop Sell under each holding is not worth placing; the brake that holds less when the whole basket gets jumpy is what actually protects them.

insights.title: Raw residual momentum under an own-volatility target (M0007-N20-RAW + M0001 overlay) starts paper trading as RM-FR
insights.body: Sera picked this method to trade with pretend money every night, under the short name RM-FR, taking the place of FND. Its rules are now locked, and its record starts from its first night on paper, so nothing before that counts. Month by month against SPY is how it earns trust.

insights.title: Checking the momentum book every week instead of every month costs nothing
insights.body: We ran the best stock-picking book with a weekly check that keeps the same monthly list but nudges every holding back to an equal share each week. It came out the same as checking once a month: about 15% a year either way, the same worst fall and the same luck score. So a weekly signal can be added to this book without paying extra in costs or lost return, which opens the door to ideas that need to react faster than once a month. The weekly safety exit we were testing at the same time did not work: selling a falling stock and buying it back a week later during a market-wide drop just sold it again lower.

insights.title: A brake that checks weekly how wildly the stocks swing makes the best book safer at no cost
insights.body: The braked momentum book on paper decides once a month how much to hold, based on how wildly its stocks swung over the past month. Checking that same brake every week, while still picking the stocks once a month, cut its worst fall from 14% to 12% with almost no loss of return, and only 4 more trades in 20 years. It works because it trims all holdings a little as the swings grow, before most of a fall, and adds back as they calm, without selling any particular stock. Everything that sold after prices fell (safety exits under each stock, a brake on the whole basket, a weekly market switch) did worse, because it sold near the bottom and missed the rebound. For the owner: a weekly check of this kind is worth doing; it means adjusting how much you hold once a week, not picking new stocks.

insights.title: RM's book with its volatility brake re-read every week starts paper trading as RMW-FR
insights.body: Sera picked this method to trade with pretend money every night, under the short name RMW-FR, taking the place of RM-FR. Its rules are now locked, and its record starts from its first night on paper, so nothing before that counts. Month by month against SPY is how it earns trust.
